January 28, 1986. 11:38 in the morning.
The space shuttle Challenger lifts off from Florida… and millions of Americans are watching live.
Seven astronauts on board. Among them, a teacher… who was supposed to give the first lesson from space.
Seventy-three seconds later… the shuttle turned into a cloud of smoke and fire.
No survivors.
The question investigators spent months on: how does the most important space program in the world fall… because of a piece of rubber less than one centimeter thick?
And worse: why did the shuttle launch at all… when engineers had warned the night before?

Let's start with the two side boosters. Each booster is built from segments stacked on top of each other.
Between every two segments, two rubber rings called "O-rings"… their job is to seal the gap, so the burning gases can't leak.
The gas inside the booster is hotter than three thousand degrees.
And the problem wasn't new. For years, boosters had come back from flights with burn marks on their rings.
In January 1985, on a flight launched at twelve degrees, clear damage was found on the rings.
And in July 1985, engineer Roger Boisjoly wrote an internal memo… warning that a failure could lead to "a catastrophe of the highest order… and loss of human life."
But the flights went on.

On the evening of January 27, Florida is bitterly cold.
The forecast: temperatures below freezing overnight… and ice covering the launch pad.
Engineers at Morton Thiokol, the company that built the boosters, call for an urgent teleconference with NASA.
Their recommendation is clear: no launch below twelve degrees. Cold rubber stiffens… and doesn't seal the gap in time.
But NASA officials pushed back on the recommendation.
The company's managers asked for a short break… and met away from the engineers.
They came back with a new decision: launch is possible.
The engineers never changed their minds. But the decision was no longer theirs.

On launch morning, the air temperature was just two degrees.
Less than a second after ignition, puffs of black smoke appeared at a joint on the right booster.
The cold ring had not sealed the joint. But burnt residue plugged the gap for a while… so the climb continued.
About fifty-eight seconds in, a small flame appeared on that same side… pointing toward the external tank full of fuel.
At second seventy-three, the tank failed… and the shuttle broke apart in the sky.
Seven astronauts. Seven families. And a whole country watching live.

The President ordered an official investigation… a commission led by former Secretary of State William Rogers.
At one public hearing, physicist Richard Feynman ran a simple experiment.
He put a piece of O-ring rubber in a glass of ice water… then squeezed it and took it out.
The rubber did not spring back. It stayed compressed for seconds.
An experiment that took less than a minute… showed the whole world what happened on launch morning.
But the commission didn't stop at the rubber.

In June 1986, the Rogers Commission released its final report.
The direct cause: failure of the O-rings in the right booster joint, due to a flawed design… made worse by the cold.
The deeper cause: a flawed decision-making process. Those who approved the launch didn't know the history of O-ring problems… or the engineers' written recommendation against launching.
Feynman wrote in an appendix to the report: "Nature cannot be fooled."
Shuttle flights stopped for thirty-two months… until the joint was redesigned.
It wasn't just the fault of a piece of rubber. It was a warning that arrived in time… and went unheard.
